system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for observation following his third transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) procedure targeting residual tumors in liver segments VI, VII, and VIII. The procedure was successfully performed via the right femoral artery, delivering doxorubicin-eluting beads to the tumor sites. A previously suspected phrenic artery supply was not identified, but a feeding vessel from the right adrenal/intercostal artery was successfully coiled and embolized to prevent non-target perfusion. The patient tolerated the procedure well, with no immediate complications, pain, or bleeding at the access site. He remained stable throughout the admission, with mild expected changes in liver enzymes. He was discharged home the following day with instructions to monitor for post-embolization syndrome, continue all home medications, and follow up with oncology and hepatology in four weeks for imaging and treatment reassessment.
problems: Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old man with multifocal HCC s/p TACE. // RFA to residual
tumor and 2 additional sites.

OPERATORS:  Dr ___ imaging fellow) and Dr ___
radiologist) performed the procedure. The attending radiologist was present
and supervising throughout the entirety of the procedure.

DOSE:  676 mGy-cm

FINDINGS: 

Limited preprocedure CT scan of the abdomen was performed for purposes of RFA
planning. This demonstrated a sidewall in the abdomen segment 7 lesion. The
portion enhancing on prior MRI to not contain a sidewall, which were targeted
for RFA ablation. The additional 2 segment 8 lesions to be targeted are not
well visualized on noncontrast examination.

Findings of cirrhosis liver with splenomegaly and collateral vessels. Right
renal cysts. Gallstones.

Arterial imaging of the abdomen was later performed after administration of
100cc of IV contrast material after the first ablation was completed.

COMPARISON:  Abdomen from ___ and chemoembolization from ___.

SEDATION:  General anesthesia was administered by the anesthesiologist
department. Please see their notes for dedicated details.

PROCEDURE:  Radiofrequency ablation of the segment 7 residual lesion.

TECHNIQUE:  The risks, benefits and alternatives of the procedure were
explained to the patient and informed written consent was obtained. An
approach to ablation was determined with the patient in a supine position and
the access site was marked with ink on the patient's skin surface. A
pre-procedure timeout was then performed using three patient identifiers was
performed per ___ protocol.

The access site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. A 20 cm
length cluster radiofrequency ablation probe was advanced into the liver to
the targeted segment 7 lesion, its medial and inferior portion under CT
guidance. Confirmation of its position was performed under CT fluoroscopy.
Radiofrequency ablation was then performed for a total of 12 min with maximal
temperature of 88 degrees Celsius. During the ablation of this lesion, the
ablation was halted 2 times for hypertension due to irritation of the
immediately adjacent adrenal gland. Blood pressure was monitored and
controlled by the anesthesia team. Once blood pressure was in an acceptable
range, the ablation continued for a total of 12 min.

The cluster probe was then slowly withdrawn and readjusted into the superior
portion of the medial aspect of the lesion and ablation was then performed for
an additional 10 min with maximal temperature of 88 degrees Celsius. The
ablation probe was then removed, with low energy ablation of the tract
performed along the way. A limited, arterial CT of the abdomen was then
performed after administration of 100 mL of IV contrast material to locate the
additional 2 segment 8 lesions and to assess the ablation coverage of the
segment 7 lesion as the segment 8 lesions are not visible under ultrasound. At
this time, it was noted that there was new free fluid surrounding the liver
and to a lesser extent along the inferior spleen and right paracolic gutter.
There is high-density material along the ablation tract extending into the
subcapsular region, compatible with hemorrhage. The patient's blood pressure
was slightly hypotensive at this time, which was managed by the anesthesia
department. It is unclear whether the slightly low blood pressures were due to
the hemorrhage or due to the control of the recent hypertension. The decision
was made to terminate the procedure at this time and take the patient to the
angiography suite for embolization of the bleed. The patient left the
department in stable condition.

IMPRESSION: 

1. Successful radiofrequency ablation of the residual segment 7 tumor.

2. The patient became hypertensive during the ablation of the segment 7 tumor
due to its immediate proximity to the adrenal gland, which was controlled by
the anesthesiology department.

3. At the conclusion of the segment 7 ablation after the probe was removed,
limited imaging through the area demonstrated arterial extravasation from the
ablation tract. The decision was made to terminate the procedure without
ablating the additional two segment 8 lesions and instead go to the
angiography suite for embolization.

4. Please see dedicated dictation for full details on the embolization
procedure.

INDICATION:  ___ MALE WITH ACTIVE BLEEDING ON POST RFA CT.  HEPATIC
ARTERY ANGIOGRAM AND EMBOLIZATION REQUESTED.

COMPARISON:  Same day CT abdomen and chemoembolization of the liver ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ (interventional radiology fellow) and
Dr. ___ (interventional radiology attending) performed the procedure.
The attending was present and supervising throughout the procedure.

ANESTHESIA: General anesthesia was provided for the duration today's case.  1%
lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the
access site

CONTRAST: 125 ml of Optiray contrast.

FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 29.5 min, 1168 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Right common femoral artery access.

2. Common hepatic digital subtraction arteriogram and 3D CT

3. Digital subtraction angiogram of right middle adrenal artery.

4. Right common femoral artery closed using Angio Seal device.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:

Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the
procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the patient's wife as
the patient was already under general anesthesia for the ___ procedure.. The
patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the
exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___ protocol. The
right groin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Using palpatory and fluoroscopic guidance, the right common femoral artery was
punctured using a micropuncture set at the level of the mid-femoral head. A
0.018 wire was passed easily into the vessel lumen. A small skin incision was
made over the needle. Then the inner dilator and wire were removed and a
___ wire was advanced under fluoroscopy into the aorta. The micropuncture
sheath was exchanged for a 5 ___ sheath which was attached to a continuous
heparinized saline side arm flush.

A C2 Cobra glide catheter was advanced over ___ wire into the aorta. The
wire was removed and the celiac artery was selectively cannulated and a small
contrast injection was made to confirm position. A glidewire was then advanced
into the common hepatic artery and a Glide catheter advanced to the common
hepatic artery. A digital subtraction angiogram and 3D spin CT was performed.

3D CT was performed under the direct supervision of the attending supervision.
Reformatted images were obtained using a separate workstation. The information
gained from these reformatted images were crucial in the success of the case.

At this time the Cobra catheter was removed and ___ catheter advanced
over the ___ wire and formed in the aorta. The ___ catheter was used
to select out the right renal artery which had a common trunk of the right
middle adrenal artery and right phrenic artery. Digital subtraction angiogram
was performed. A combination of micro catheters and micro wires were used in
an attempt to further select out the adrenal and phrenic arteries, however,
all were unsuccessful.

The catheter was then removed over the wire and the sheath was removed.
Angioseal device was used to achieve hemostasis of the right common femoral
artery puncture site. Sterile dressings were applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  No immediate complications. Patient
transferred to the PACU.

FINDINGS: 

1. DSA and 3D CT of the common hepatic artery demonstrated no evidence of
active extravasation.

2. DSA of right renal artery ostium containing take-offs of the right middle
adrenal artery and right phrenic artery demonstrate no evidence of active
extravasation.

3. Angio Seal device placed for closure.

IMPRESSION: 

No evidence of active extravasation demonstrated during today's procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’re in the recovery area after your procedure. You had a radiofrequency ablation for one of the liver tumors, but there was some bleeding afterward. We did a scan that showed blood leaking near the ablation site, so you were taken to angiography to check for the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bleeding? Is it serious? I don’t feel any pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was concerning at the time. You became a bit hypotensive, so we gave you medication to support your blood pressure and briefly placed a breathing tube to keep you stable. But the good news is, the angiogram didn’t show any active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So they couldn’t find where it was coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The interventional radiologist checked the hepatic artery and even the adrenal and phrenic arteries nearby, but no active extravasation was seen. That means the bleeding likely stopped on its own or was sealed off when the probe was removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the last time I had a procedure, it went smoothly. Why did this happen now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: During the ablation of the tumor in segment 7, the probe was very close to the adrenal gland. That caused a temporary spike in blood pressure, which the anesthesia team managed. When the probe was pulled out, that’s when we saw signs of bleeding on the CT. To be safe, we stopped the rest of the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the other tumors weren’t treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We focused on controlling the bleeding. The segment 7 tumor was successfully ablated, but the two in segment 8 weren’t touched. We’ll discuss next steps with your oncology team in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m glad it’s under control. What about my blood pressure now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well now. Your blood pressure has been stable since we weaned off the pressors. We’re monitoring you closely overnight just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your hemoglobin is stable at 10.8, and liver enzymes are a bit elevated but expected after the ablation. We’re planning to discharge you today if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Should I expect more pain or bleeding at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might have some soreness at the rib site where the probe went in. We’re giving you a small supply of oxycodone for breakthrough pain, but avoid it if you’re drowsy or confused. Watch for increasing pain, fever, or dizziness—those would be reasons to call or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my usual medications? I take furosemide and spironolactone for my liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held those overnight because of the blood pressure concerns, but you can restart them today as prescribed. All your other medications—nadolol, aspirin, omeprazole, glyburide—are back on schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see hepatology and oncology in about four weeks for imaging to check the ablation site and plan further treatment. Also, please get a repeat CBC as an outpatient to monitor your blood count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well through a complicated situation. We’ll make sure your care team has all the details. You’re cleared to go home when you’re ready.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted after experiencing post-procedural bleeding following a radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of a liver tumor in segment 7. A CT scan revealed arterial extravasation from the ablation tract, prompting transfer to the angiography suite. Angiography showed no active bleeding, and the patient was briefly hypotensive, requiring pressors and temporary intubation before stabilization. The procedure was terminated without treating two additional tumors in segment 8. He remained hemodynamically stable overnight with no further bleeding. His diuretics were held initially but restarted at discharge, and home medications were continued. He was discharged home the following day with instructions to monitor for complications and follow up with oncology and hepatology in four weeks for treatment reassessment.
